source.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
source.authors: Srikanth Malla; Chi-Ho Choi; J. Choi

page_placements.theme: Off-target steering induces refusal (refusal as a fallback state)

record.tranche_reason: The study derives a refusal behavior direction by difference of means and tests adding it, but uses contrastive behavior examples and a single selected layer rather than the original harmful/harmless setup and all-layer ablation.
record.gate_note: The refusal-specific results are the direction's held-out decodability and its effect when added. The paper's broader interference and random-push results do not directly test the refusal-direction ablation, harmful-request compliance, or capability-preservation parts of the claim.
record.test_reason: This is a weak, indirect test. The study builds a difference-of-means refusal direction and adds it at one layer on neutral prompts. That direction contrasts refusing and helping responses to the same prompt, mean-pooled over response tokens; it is not a harmful-minus-harmless instruction contrast. Judge-rated refusal rises. The study also shows that norm-matched random directions induce refusal, more than any other behavior. Together these bear on the addition part of V1 and on how specific it is. There is no ablation, no harmful prompts and no capability check.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that steering side effects are set by the model's defaults, not by the geometry of the steered direction. Random norm-matched pushes reproduce real steers' induced-behavior ranking (rho 0.90 on Qwen2.5-7B, weaker in each family's largest model), and geometry predicts held-out interference poorly (Spearman ≤0.41, R2 <0.10).
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-of-means directions and activation addition, but derives them from synthetic behavior-present/absent response pairs and applies the steer at one selected layer. It does not test all-layer removal or the original harmful/harmless refusal setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The random-push correspondence weakens in the largest models in each family; the reported attractor correlation is 0.54 for Qwen2.5-72B, 0.38 for Llama-3.3-70B, and 0.15 for Gemma-2-27B. The specific behaviors induced also vary by model.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal is a leading 'attractor sink': many unrelated behavior steers induce refusal as a side effect, and in most refusal-trained families refusal is the top steer-induced behavior. In Mistral it is the weakest.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Off-target activation perturbations of any kind push refusal-trained chat models toward refusal; refusal works as a default fallback state.

record.problems: The refusal-specific causal evidence is limited to one model and a one-layer addition measured by a language-model judge on neutral prompts. The study does not test removal or general capability preservation. Its detailed map uses 32 evaluation prompts and synthetic contrastive examples; each model judges its own generations in the main cross-model study.

untested.parts: Ablation or removal of the direction; harmful-instruction compliance; preservation of general capabilities; harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction; all-layer projection.
All for refusal. The 3-dim cone is used only as a predictor of interference.
All. Sec. 8 only remarks that refusal is the top steer-induced behavior in refusal-trained families but the weakest in Mistral.

missing.what: Refusal's source-strength rank as a significant sink (among the top three, with sycophancy and poeticism) on Qwen2.5-7B, with bootstrap interval.
Per-model effect of a random push on refusal across the ten models, and the statement that refusal is the leading induced behavior in refusal-trained families but the weakest in Mistral.
Whether the refusal direction was steerable, and its self-effect, in the other nine models. Only steerable counts are given.

record.verdict_notes: The refusal direction is one of 24 synthetic response-contrast behaviors and is not the original harmful/harmless instruction setup. The direction's measured self-effect is constrained by coefficient calibration, so it cannot show the strength of the effect. The random-push result, where refusal is what random directions induce most, is the most relevant finding for V1: it suggests that 'adding a direction induces refusal' is partly non-specific in this setting.

versions.untested_parts: Tests adding a refusal direction at one selected layer on neutral prompts. Does not test removal, projection at every layer and position, compliance with harmful requests, or preservation of general capabilities. The refusal direction is derived from behavior-present/absent contrastive responses, not specifically harmful versus harmless instructions.
Weight-edit or abliteration removal in released models.
Jailbreak suppression of the refusal direction and training against its ablation.
Whether refusal itself is represented by an affine set, cone, or dominant direction plus other refusal directions.
Separation between harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
How refusal-training method or timing determines whether a removable direction exists.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Held-out projection AUROC for the refusal difference-of-means direction
rows.measure: AUROC for distinguishing refusal-present from refusal-absent responses
rows.note: This establishes that the refusal behavior is linearly decodable; by itself it does not establish causal mediation.
rows.check: Selection value, not a test. The layer (7) was picked from layers 7–23 as the one with the highest held-out AUROC, and all 24 behaviors reach 1.00. It shows decodability only, which the paper says does not imply steerability. It has no bearing on V1's causal claim.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Added the raw refusal difference-of-means direction through a forward hook at its selected layer
rows.measure: Change in judge-rated refusal self-effect on a 0-to-10 scale
rows.baseline: Unsteered generations on the same prompts
rows.note: The paper reports this as the refusal direction's calibrated self-effect; the measure is a judge rating, not a refusal rate.
rows.check: The value is partly a selection value. The coefficient was calibrated so the self-effect lands closest to a 2-point target, with a 1-point floor. So +1.81 shows a coherent coefficient exists that induces refusal, but its size is set by design. Other caveats: the direction is a response-level refusal-vs-help contrast, not harmful-minus-harmless instructions. Prompts are neutral, the readout is a self-judge's 0–10 rating, and the baseline is unsteered generation.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix D, Table 3 (refusal: layer 7, AUROC 1.00, shuffled 0.47, coefficient 2, self-effect +1.81, coherence 0.98, steerable yes); App. D protocol (raw DiM vector, forward hook, every position, greedy, 48 tokens, 32 neutral prompts, self-judge)
source_check.problem: All fields match. Observed is defensible because refusal clears the floor from a near-zero baseline, but the coefficient was picked to land closest to a 2-point target, so the size cannot show full induction.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Added random directions matched to real steers in added norm

conditions.value: held to the same coherence bar as real steers

rows.value: Figure only; text says random pushes significantly induce refusal
rows.note: This is a random-push result, not an effect of the refusal behavior direction.
rows.check: Should link to V1 as a specificity control for the addition claim. Random norm-matched directions significantly induce refusal, and refusal is the behavior a random push induces most (Sec. 6). The refusal effect size of the random push is shown only in a figure; no number is given in the text.

source_check.locator_found: Sec. 6 (random push significantly induces ten behaviors, led by refusal; refusal is what a random push induces most); Fig. 3b; App. F (24 random directions); Sec. 3 Step 4 (norm-matched, same coherence floor)
source_check.problem: Correct as a control row. The text gives no number for refusal under random push and does not compare it with the refusal direction's +1.81.

relationships.condition: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, neutral prompts, one-layer addition (layer 7, coefficient 2), self-judge rating
relationships.reason: Adding the refusal direction raises judge-rated refusal (+1.81, coefficient calibrated to a ~2-point target, r2). Norm-matched random directions also significantly induce refusal, more than any other behavior (r3). So induction by addition here is not specific to the refusal direction.
relationships.display_finding: Adding the refusal direction increased judge-rated refusal by 1.81, but norm-matched random directions also significantly induced refusal.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, neutral prompts, one-layer addition (layer 7, coefficient 2), self-judge rating
labels.reason: Adding the direction does induce refusal (+1.81, r2), so challenges is not warranted. 24 norm-matched random directions also significantly induce refusal, more than any other behavior (r3), so induction is not unique to the direction. The text gives no size comparison, so specificity is unshown rather than disproven; the record's 'not specific' slightly overstates this.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on whether adding a DiM refusal direction induces refusal and whether random directions do too. The test is weak and indirect: the direction comes from response contrasts and the magnitude is calibration-capped.

tranche.reason: The study's question is steering interference across 24 behaviors, not refusal mediation, so T2 (same question) does not fit. It does report a result on V1's addition arm in a new setting: a refusal direction built from response contrasts, one-layer addition, neutral prompts, a self-judge and a norm-matched random control.

source_check.notes: The refusal direction comes from 12 synthetic refusing-vs-helping response triples, mean-pooled over response tokens; it is not harmful-minus-harmless instructions. It is added at every position at layer 7, the lower edge of the 7-23 search band. There is no ablation and no capability measure beyond a distinct-bigram coherence floor of 0.6. The Sec. 8 cross-model refusal result (refusal leads in most models of Qwen/Llama/Gemma, weakest of seven in Mistral-7B) has no row. The authors_conclusion paraphrase is accurate.

statements.correction: 2609.06951, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: the direction contrasts refusing and helping responses, not harmful and harmless instructions. Added at layer 7 with coefficient 2 on 32 neutral prompts, with the model as its own judge, it raises judge-rated refusal by +1.81 on the 0-10 scale. 24 norm-matched random directions also significantly induce refusal, more than any other behavior. No magnitude comparison is given. This supports limits_scope, not challenges.
statements.problem: The sentence about this study is accurate. But it is filed under 'controls match the effect' with label challenges. The text never compares the random push's refusal induction with the refusal direction's own effect, so a match is not shown. The effect is not absent (+1.81), and the record's verdict is limits_scope.

statements.correction: 2609.06951 tests addition, not ablation. Random norm-matched pushes significantly induce refusal on Qwen2.5-7B, with no size comparison to the refusal direction's +1.81 judge points. Setting: 32 neutral prompts, self-judge, coefficient closest to a 2-point target with a 1-point floor and coherence above 0.6. What weakens is attractor rho: 0.90 on Qwen2.5-7B, against Qwen2.5-72B 0.54, Llama-3.3-70B 0.38 and Gemma-2-27B 0.15.
statements.problem: This study is listed as 'not specific' under a question about removal, but it tests only induction by addition. Its random control is not shown to match the steer's size. 'Random-push effect weakening' really means the rank correlation between random-push and real-steer induction weakens.

statements.correction: 2609.06951 does not test removal by ablation or a weight edit. Its only V1 result is induction by one-layer addition, with verdict limits_scope.
statements.problem: The pack truncates this statement, and the visible text makes no claim about this study and cites no rows from it. The study tests addition only and has a limits_scope verdict, so it should not count toward removal support or the supports tally.

statements.correction: Qwen2.5-7B: refusal is among the ten significant sinks, led by sycophancy, refusal and poeticism, and is what a random push induces most. Sec. 8: refusal leads in most models of the three refusal-trained families (Qwen, Llama, Gemma). In Mistral-7B it is the weakest of its seven.
statements.problem: Right in substance but loose. The text says 'most models of the three refusal-trained families', not 'most families'. In Mistral refusal is 'the weakest of its seven', not the weakest overall. The cross-model result is not in cited row r3, which covers only Qwen2.5-7B under random push.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Adding the refusal difference-of-means direction to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at layer 7 on neutral prompts
reader_labels.reason: The addition increases the judge-rated refusal self-effect by +1.81 points, supporting the addition component in this tested setting (r2).
